classification.difficultyReason: Parts a-d are scaffolded: cube a negative number, then reverse it to get the cube root. The only new idea is sign handling for odd powers. Part e, ∛(-125), is unscaffolded but is a single recognition step. It is a little more than direct evaluation of positive powers and roots, and less than a mixed set that needs matching or comparing.

classification.difficultyReason: The task is split into three steps. The student evaluates a square root and a cube root of a negative, handles the sign, and multiplies two fractions. It is a routine linked chain with a few decisions. It is above simple compare-and-notice questions but below the varied fraction, decimal and mixed-number evaluations in p47-q8, which has no scaffolding.

classification.difficultyReason: The student must decide for each part whether the same-base multiplication law applies. Part b is a sum and part c has different bases. Where it applies, the work is one routine step, with one negative index in part d. It is harder than p49-q3, which is pure application. It is easier than p49-q4, which adds fractional, pronumeral and mixed-base cases.

classification.difficultyReason: The three parts are signposted: factorise 18, apply (ab)^n = a^n × b^n to 2 × 3², then simplify (3²)³. The student links the product-power and power-of-power rules, with a non-prime base kept as 3² in part b. That is more than the direct power-of-power fill-ins. It is less than p54-q4, which needs the student to see and write the factorisation themselves.

questions.mappingNote: apply-index-laws-numerical is the primary skill recorded on this master question; its audit-v2 review is current for this content.

classification.difficultyReason: The numbers are already given in prime-factor form, and part a scaffolds the alignment of bases with zero powers. The student then takes minimum powers for the HCF and maximum powers for the LCM across three numbers. The LCM needs a modest multiplication. This is a routine linked procedure, slightly more than p72-q1 because there are three numbers and zero powers to handle. It is a bit below the variation block, which asks for predictions about what changes.
